newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon leads Arab world in cellular phone usage.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon leads Arab world in cellular phone usage.

text.p: Lebanon leads the Arab world in cellular telephone subscriptions and has the world's lowest airtime tariffs, cellular telephone company Libancell said on Wednesday.

Hussein Rifai, chairman of Libancell, told delegates at an international conference on developments in the Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) that Lebanon had 180,000 subscribers to Libancell and rival firm Cellis.

Saudi Arabia came second with 165,000 subscribers, followed by three other Gulf states: the United Arab Emirates with 105,000, Kuwait with 60,000 and Qatar with 23,000. Bahrain and Jordan have 19,000 and 15,000 subscribers respectively.
Rifai said a cellular network was on trial in Tunisia and networks were being set up in Egypt, Libya, Oman, Sudan and Syria.
There was a rush to GSM in Lebanon due to the lack of sufficient fixed network lines, Rifai said.
"Lebanon now with 18 months of operation has the highest number of subscribers with the two operational networks," he told the delegates to the four-day Pan-Arab Technical Seminar.

Libancell and its rival Cellis were set up by Finland Telecom and France Telecom. With Lebanon's war-damaged telephone network undergoing repair and expansion, the two firms won bids in 1994 to install systems for 300,000 cellular telephones each.
"Our network capacity will reach 100,000 lines by the year end. We have now roaming operational with 22 operators in 21 countries," Rifai added.
Lebanon's airtime tarrif of five cents per minute was rock bottom and Lebanese subscribers were extremely talkative, he said.

"I believe we have the lowest airtime tarrifs in the whole world. The Lebanese subscriber is quite distinguished by extremely high talk time. We are currently measuring after 18 months of operation between 800 and 1,000 minutes of use (per month) compared I think to European averages of 130 to 200.

"Lebanese subscribers are prestige and social status conscious, seeking nice numbers and are gadget-oriented... Whenever you go to restaurants here you find plenty of cellular telephones lying on the tables," Rifai added.
